channel.title: The Dig — HPC-QC integration and resource management
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the HPC-QC integration and resource management preset. Today’s ranked reading list covers three adjacent software-stack concerns rather than spin-qubit hardware itself: 2611.15080 offers a structure-aware equivalence-checking oracle for validating unitary circuit transformations, 2611.16285 reports multi-GPU orchestration for relay belief-propagation QEC decoding on an HPC system, and 2611.16971 presents a low-cost, hardware-agnostic zero-noise extrapolation wrapper for NISQ error mitigation. No pay dirt today — 1 to skim.

item.title: Scaling Pêlagos: Multi-GPU Orchestration for Relay Belief-Propagation Decoding
item.description:
Skim incremental — Process-isolated orchestration achieves eight-GPU end-to-end speedups of 5.68× (MI300X) and 6.23× (MI355X) on one-gross ([[144,12,12]]) circuits, and 6.92× and 7.01× on two-gross ([[288,12,18]]) circuits. Isolated GPU decoding time alone yields 7.58× and 7.45× speedups on the two-gross code.

Grade 0.507 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computers for High-Performance Computing”

Figure

End-to-end and GPU-only scaling speedup as a function of GPU count (1, 2, 4, 8) normalized to single-GPU throughput, comparing baseline multi-GPU Pêlagos to the process-isolated implementation across one-gross and two-gross codes.

Asks

How can host-side orchestration bottlenecks be eliminated to achieve near-linear multi-GPU scaling for Pêlagos relay belief-propagation decoding on single-node GPU clusters?

Before

Original Pêlagos used a single host Python process managing multiple HIP device contexts with serial preprocessing; the new design improves eight-GPU throughput over this baseline by >2× on one-gross, and by 1.48× (MI300X) and 1.36× (MI355X) on two-gross.

But

Fixed batch size of 1,024 syndromes per GPU; maximum batch bounded by signed 32-bit indexing (E×B≤231−1); circuit-level depolarizing noise at physical error rate p=0.003 and relay limit R=50.

Tools

Pêlagos Relay-BP decoder · AMD Instinct MI300X and MI355X GPUs · Process-isolated HIP contexts · Host shared-memory output collection · Bivariate bicycle codes

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum error-correction (QEC) decoders that achieve low logical error rates under real-time operating constraints. These constraints motivate heuristic decoding algorithms whose error-correction performance must be evaluated through large-scale simulation. High-throughput decoding accelerates this evaluation and the exploration of decoder parameters. Using multiple graphics processing units (GPUs) is a natural way to scale these simulations, but naively distributing syndrome batches introduces host-side preprocessing and output-collection overheads that limit scaling. To address these limitations, we extend the Pêlagos relay belief-propagation (Relay-BP) decoder with process-isolated orchestration, parallel host preprocessing, and shared-memory output. We evaluate both one-gross ([[144,12,12]]) and two-gross ([[288,12,18]]) codes in a multi-GPU environment. Specifically, for the one-gross circuit at R=50, eight AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and eight AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs achieve optimized end-to-end speedups of 5.68× and 6.23×, respectively. For the two-gross circuit, the corresponding speedups are 6.92× and 7.01×. When throughput is calculated using GPU decoding time, the corresponding two-gross speedups are 7.58× and 7.45×, indicating near-linear GPU scaling. We deploy Pêlagos on Lux, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's AMD Instinct MI355X-based supercomputer, as a pathfinding application for high-throughput QEC simulation. This deployment provides a concrete quantum-computing use case for the AI + HPC infrastructure supporting the Genesis Mission's scientific-discovery goals. These end-to-end measurements demonstrate a practical path to accelerating large-scale QEC simulation through efficient multi-GPU decoding.

arxave:action.title: Assess Relay-BP orchestration for spin-qubit QEC offload

item.arxave:action: Evaluate whether the process-isolated shard orchestration and shared-memory output pattern can be reused when routing syndrome decoding from the spin-qubit QPU to HPC GPUs, including compatibility with our control stack and latency budget.

Ask the authors whether the orchestration was evaluated only for offline QEC simulation or also under live syndrome-streaming latency constraints, and what host-GPU communication overhead remains for real-time decoding.

arxave:action.title: No spin-qubit or live integration results

item.arxave:action: The paper benchmarks offline QEC simulation on Lux and does not report live syndrome streaming, spin-qubit readout, calibration integration, or real-time decoder latency, so benefits for our machine are indirect.
